headline: OpenHands’ writable, shell-capable runtime paired with gpt-researcher’s broad egress and MCP creates medium-to-high risks of leakage, prompt injection, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-researcher can ingest local documents and web content, while OpenHands can use MCP and read/write runtime files. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from A can be passed into B and treated as instructions. The pair is not provably isolated, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF gpt-researcher writes fetched content into files that OpenHands later reads
IF OpenHands consumes MCP or file content as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable shared folders between the two runtimes
Require provenance tags on any file passed from A to B
Add a prompt-injection scanner before B reads A-produced text
Use separate MCP servers per agent
requires-engineering: enforce content-type allowlists in the orchestrator

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-researcher touches local documents and secrets, and OpenHands can read mounted files plus use broad network egress. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, sensitive research material from A can flow into B and then out through B’s networked tools. The shared-volume path is plausible from the profiles, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents are attached to the same mounted workspace
IF A places secrets or local documents into files that B can read
IF B forwards those files to external APIs or websites
mitigations: Mount separate workspaces for each agent
Move secrets out of any shared directory
Block outbound network from B for sensitive runs
Review runtime mounts before starting the pair
requires-engineering: add per-file data-loss prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and shell execution; gpt-researcher can also read files and spawn subprocesses, with multiple instances supported. If both operate on the same repo or directory, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide and corrupt state. The profiles do not show locking, so the safer high severity applies.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or directory
IF either agent commits or rewrites files while the other is active
IF no external lock or queue serializes writes
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent
Serialize git operations through one operator
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use read-only mode for gpt-researcher outputs
requires-engineering: add filesystem locking around shared paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-researcher produces research reports and citations, and OpenHands can act in a shell/editor loop. That makes it plausible for B to treat A’s output as authoritative and then execute or commit based on it. Because the profiles do not show a verification gate, the interaction is risky in default workflows.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses gpt-researcher output as task input without review
IF A’s citations or facts are copied into B’s action plan
IF B is allowed to execute shell commands or commits from that plan
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A’s report
Add a verification step against source URLs
Limit B to drafting only, not execution
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
requires-engineering: implement structured handoff validation

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and docs-only, with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch stated. The only concrete compliance-relevant difference is that OpenHands handles mounted runtime files while gpt-researcher handles local documents and API keys, but the profiles do not prove a regulated-data mismatch. One-agent citations are sufficient because no cross-agent compliance breach is evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared runtime
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared runtime
Document retention settings for both agents
Use separate environments for sensitive and non-sensitive work
Review vendor terms before deployment
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing
